:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: If $x = y + 2y\sqrt y$, find $\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx}$ at the point $\left(3 , 1\right).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y+2y\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y+2{y}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3/2}) \\  & =1+2\cdot (\frac{3}{2}{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =1+3{y}^{1/2} \\  & =1+3\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy},$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \left( \dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy} \right)^{-1} =  \dfrac{1}{1 + 3\sqrt y}.
$$

Finally, substituting the point $(3,1),$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(3,1)} & =\frac{1}{1+3\sqrt{1}}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: What is the equation of the tangent to the curve $x = 2y^2 -y + 1$ at the point $(2,1)?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(2{y}^{2}-y+1) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =2\cdot (2y)-1+0 \\  & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy},$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \left( \dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac1{4y - 1}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(2,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(2,1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-2) \\ y & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}+1 \\ y & =\frac{x}{3}+\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Equation of a Tangent Line Using dx/dy

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that a curve is defined by the following equation:

$$
x= y^3+y
$$

We say that the equation of this curve is defined **implicitly** because instead of the usual $y = y(x),$ we have $x = x(y).$ Sometimes, it's convenient to define a curve this way. You'll meet more implicit curves later.

To graph this curve, we can start by selecting some values of $y$ and computing the corresponding $x$-values as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y=0 & \quad \longrightarrow\quad  x=0^3+0=0 \\[5pt]
	y=1 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x=1^3+1=2  \\[5pt]
	y=2 & \quad\longrightarrow\quad x=2^3+2=10 \\[5pt]
\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the points $(0,0),$ $(2,1),$ and $(10,2).$ If we plot these points and connect them with a smooth curve, we get the following graph:

Plotting this curve in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](images/81/812db123dd422ff781472c73156a2f4d6e88a99aa3726668cd7a8b8882d6e0a8.png)

To find the slope of the tangent to this curve at a point, we need to follow two steps.

- First, we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy}$ by differentiating the equation of the curve with respect to $y.$

- Then, we find $\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx}$ by taking the reciprocal of $\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy}{:}$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \left( \dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac1{\left(\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy}\right)}
$$

We'll explore some intuition behind this result at the end of the lesson, but for now, let's focus on carrying out the computation.

We start by differentiating $x=y^3+y$ with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}+y) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y) \\  & =3{y}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take its reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative is also defined implicitly. In other words, $\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx}$ is a function of $y,$ not $x.$

To calculate the slope of the tangent to this curve at a point, say $(2,{\color{blue}{1}}),$ we substitute ${\color{blue}{y}} = {\color{blue}{1}}$ into our expression for $\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(2,1)} & =\frac{1}{3(1)^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(2,1)$ equals $\dfrac14.$

\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-2) \\ y & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}+1 \\ y & =\frac{x}{3}+\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Equation of a Tangent Line Using dx/dy

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Throughout this lesson, we've made use of the following result:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \left( \dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy} \right)^{-1}
$$

Let's now build some more intuition behind this result.

Consider the graph of $x=f(y),$ shown below.

![](images/f1/f11b52c2b788fcf1a9a161fa46843d42c10973545f2ff923750bcb4c50b9faca.png)

The slope of the tangent to $x=f(y)$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}
$$

 

represents the change in $x$ *per unit change* in $y$ at $P.$ According to our diagram, this is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{run}}{\text{rise}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the slope of the tangent to the curve at $P$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} \\  & ={\left(\frac{\text{run}}{\text{rise}}\right)}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

This result can also be proved formally using the so-called **chain rule**.
